extracted.intended_audience: state regulatory agencies, power plant owners/operators, and environmental stakeholders (e.g., industry, NGOs, counsel) involved in implementing or commenting on EPA emission guidelines
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and applies EPA criteria and rationale used to determine the Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) and degrees of emission limitation for coal-, natural gas-, and oil-fired steam generating units (including subcategorization, compliance dates, technical feasibility, costs, and rejected options).

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural gas co-firing at 40 percent of annual heat input as BSER for medium-term coal-fired steam generating units
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is finalizing natural gas co-firing at a level of 40 percent of annual heat input as the Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) for medium-term coal-fired steam generating units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the EPA's chosen BSER for the medium-term subcategory because it is adequately demonstrated, widely applicable, cost-reasonable, reduces other air pollutants, and has limited non-air quality or energy impacts. See surrounding rationale (technical demonstration, pipeline and boiler feasibility, costs, emissions reductions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequately demonstrated — evidence for co-firing
rubrics_metrics.description: A BSER must be 'adequately demonstrated'; EPA finds co-firing at 40% adequately demonstrated because many existing coal-fired units already use natural gas and several have co-fired at or above 40% (and some at ≥60% hourly) during 2015–2020.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence includes facility reports (249 of 565 coal units reported consuming natural gas in 2021), hourly CO2 emission rate data showing units that co-fired at high shares, and historical operational experience indicating technical capability to co-fire at scale over extended periods. EPA references detailed TSD analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boiler modification feasibility and impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing coal-fired boilers can be modified to co-fire natural gas (up to 100%); typical modifications include installation of gas burners, new fuel supply lines, and air-duct modifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modifications may slightly reduce boiler efficiency (due in part to natural gas hydrogen content), but net heat rate effects can range from a 2% increase to a 2% decrease due to offsetting reduced auxiliary power demand. EPA notes common multi-fuel capability and provides timeline elements for procurement, engineering, construction, and startup in the preamble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural gas pipeline development and supply feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Supply of natural gas (via lateral pipelines) is necessary to enable co-firing at units without sufficient existing access; costs and feasibility are functions of lateral length, diameter (capacity), and proximity to transmission network.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA analyzed lateral pipeline needs for units (assuming up to 60% net summer capacity sizing to enable 40% annual co-firing), found most laterals <15 miles, estimated national incremental capacity and miles (e.g., up to ~3,500 miles, ~$11.5 billion), compared required annual pipeline construction to historical and industry-projected pipeline additions, and assessed that existing transmission systems could meet peak needs in aggregate without major transmission upgrades. Pipeline cost metric referenced: ~$280,000 per inch-mile (2019$) for lateral development within the contiguous U.S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation timeline and compliance date assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA sets a compliance date of January 1, 2030 for medium-term coal-fired steam generating units (and for natural gas- and oil-fired steam generating units) and assumes feasibility work during state plan development followed by permitting/construction after state plan effective date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assumed durations: 12 months feasibility for pipeline laterals and 6 months for boiler modifications (June 2024–June 2025); pipeline permitting and construction generally ≤3 years (June 2026–June 2029); boiler permitting 12 months, commercial arrangements ~6 months, engineering/procurement ~7 months, site work ~3 months, construction ~4 months, startup/testing ~2 months (EPA timeline and Sargent & Lundy schedule). These schedule assumptions underlie the chosen compliance date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs and cost reasonableness for co-firing
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA evaluates capital, fixed O&M, incremental fuel, and pipeline costs to determine whether co-firing is cost-reasonable; average capital cost to modify boilers to operate up to 100% natural gas is estimated at ~$52/kW and weighted average cost for 40% co-firing is estimated at ~$73/ton CO2 reduced (≈$13/MWh), amortized over 9 years in EPA's primary estimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA compares these costs to cost reasonableness metrics (e.g., emission control costs on EGUs of $10.60–$18.50/MWh and a $98/ton CO2e benchmark from a prior NSPS) and finds co-firing cost-reasonable for sources operating through Jan 1, 2039; EPA also evaluated shorter amortization periods (2–9 years) and allows states to consider RULOF adjustments for sources with fundamentally different costs. Fuel cost differential (2030 reference case) used: coal $1.56/MMBtu vs natural gas $2.95/MMBtu => $1.39/MMBtu additional fuel cost (assuming no heat rate change); EPA assumes 1% average heat rate increase in TSD.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-air quality health/environmental impacts and energy requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA assesses non-GHG emissions and energy impacts of co-firing and concludes there are no significant adverse consequences: co-firing reduces SO2, PM2.5, acid gas, mercury proportionally to reduced coal combustion; natural gas produces less NOx than coal; energy impacts on boiler efficiency are small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expected boiler efficiency decrease of 1–5% for co-firing between 20–100%, but net unit heat rate varies about ±2% due to offsetting auxiliary power reductions. EPA cites PHMSA and FERC pipeline regulations to address pipeline safety and environmental protection. EPA concludes co-firing does not have significant adverse effects on natural gas or electricity prices or on energy-sector structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of CO2 emission reductions from co-firing
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA quantifies CO2 emission reduction: approximately 4% reduction in CO2 emissions for every additional 10% of co-firing; thus moving from 100% coal to 60% coal/40% natural gas yields ~16% reduction in CO2 stack emissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This relationship supports setting the degree of emission limitation for the medium-term subcategory as a 16% reduction in emission rate (lb CO2/MWh-gross) over an extended period (e.g., annual calendar year) when BSER is 40% co-firing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology advancement expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA assesses whether designation of a BSER will drive technological advancement or cost reductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural gas co-firing is already well-established and widely used; EPA concludes the final rule is unlikely to spur major technological advances or component cost reductions for co-firing (boiler mods and pipeline construction), though broader use may improve operational efficiency for co-firing processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of CCS as BSER for medium-term coal-fired units
rubrics_metrics.description: Carbon capture and storage (CCS) is not determined to be BSER for medium-term subcategory because sources in that subcategory would have limited amortization time (less than 7 years) before their assumed cessation dates, making CCS costs exceed EPA's cost reasonableness metrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA applied amortization and cost reasonableness tests (see section VII.C.1.a.ii(D)); CCS remains BSER for long-term subcategory but is economically infeasible for medium-term units under the rule's assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of Heat Rate Improvements (HRI) as BSER for medium-term units
rubrics_metrics.description: HRI is not finalized as BSER for medium-term units because achievable CO2 reductions are low and HRIs may cause a rebound effect that could increase total emissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA cites the potential for HRI-induced operational changes leading to increased utilization and higher overall emissions; details in section VII.D.4.a of the preamble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of emission limitation for long-term coal-fired steam generating units
rubrics_metrics.description: When BSER is full-capture CCS (90% capture of CO2 in flue gas) for long-term units, EPA determines the degree of emission limitation is an 88.4% reduction in emission rate on a lb CO2/MWh-gross basis over an extended period (e.g., annual calendar year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA translates capture percentage to an emission-rate reduction (90% capture => 88.4% emission-rate reduction) to set the presumptive standard of performance on a rate basis for states to use in state plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subcategorization of natural gas- and oil-fired steam generating units by load level
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA finalizes subcategories for natural gas- and oil-fired steam generating units based on annual capacity factor: low load (<8%), intermediate load (≥8% and <45%), base load (≥45%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subcategorization reflects differences in operation, cycling, startup impacts, and emission-rate variability across load levels; the compliance date for these subcategories is January 1, 2030. EPA solicited comments and is finalizing the proposed definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER for intermediate and base load natural gas- and oil-fired steam generating units: routine methods of operation and maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is finalizing 'routine methods of operation and maintenance' as the BSER for intermediate- and base-load natural gas- and oil-fired steam generating units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: adequately demonstrated (units already operate with such practices), negligible or no additional costs (no additional technology or operational change required), no adverse non-air quality/energy impacts, and these practices prevent increases in emission rates even if they do not achieve additional CO2 reductions. EPA will set presumptive standards of performance that differ between intermediate and base load units due to operational differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSER for low-load natural gas- and oil-fired steam generating units: uniform fuels
rubrics_metrics.description: For low-load natural gas- and oil-fired steam generating units, EPA is finalizing a BSER of 'uniform fuels' with presumptive standards of performance based on heat input and depending on fuel type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: high variability in emission rates at low loads makes a BSER based on routine operation/maintenance less useful; a heat-input/fuel-composition based standard (e.g., lower-emitting fuels) provides a reasonable BSER for low-load units. EPA references prior NSPS precedent for heat-input fuel composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of alternative controls for natural gas- and oil-fired units (co-firing, CCS, hydrogen, HRI)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA considered but did not finalize other controls for natural gas- and oil-fired units: co-firing natural gas (units already fire large proportions of natural gas), CCS (high capital and operating costs relative to low utilization and low capture potential), hydrogen co-firing (limited hydrogen availability and prioritization concerns), and HRI (possible rebound effects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's reasoning includes unit utilization patterns, CO2 availability for capture, sizing/capital costs, expected tax credit magnitude (45Q) at low utilization, and limited GHG benefits given operational characteristics; thus these options do not meet BSER criteria for these subcategories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance dates for subcategories
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA finalizes compliance dates: January 1, 2030 for medium-term coal-fired steam generating units and for natural gas- and oil-fired steam generating units; CCS compliance date is January 1, 2032 for long-term coal-fired units (as discussed elsewhere).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compliance date selection is tied to EPA's implementation timeline assumptions (feasibility studies, permitting, construction) and amortization windows used in cost reasonableness analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cost reasonableness metrics and RULOF flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA evaluates cost reasonableness using benchmarks (e.g., $10.60–$18.50/MWh emission control cost range for EGUs; $98/ton CO2e from 2016 NSPS) and amortization periods, and allows states to consider RULOF (Request for Unit-Level or Other Financial) provisions where a particular source's costs differ fundamentally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA's cost findings (e.g., ~$73/ton CO2 reduced for 40% co-firing amortized over 9 years) are compared against these metrics to determine BSER cost reasonableness; state plans may use RULOF provisions to account for atypical unit economics.
